title: Penne all'Arrabbiata
subtitle: Penne in a spiced tomato sauce with garlic and chilli
excerpt: Penne all'arrabbiata is a simple Roman pasta dish: penne in a sharp, spiced tomato sauce with garlic, chilli, and good olive oil. It takes under 20 minutes and uses no onion, no meat, and no cream: the flavour comes entirely from quality tomatoes and heat.
sourceNotes: All'arrabbiata (meaning 'angry' in Italian, for the chilli heat) is a classic Roman pasta sauce. The dish originates in Lazio and has been documented in Roman trattoria cooking from the 20th century. The canonical version uses no onion and no cured meat: distinguishing it from amatriciana.

recipe.batchNotes: The sauce scales well and keeps for 5 days in the fridge. Cook pasta fresh to order.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be made 5 days ahead. Reheat, add pasta water to adjust consistency, then toss with freshly cooked penne.

glossaryTerms.definition: The starchy water drained from cooked pasta. Adding a ladleful to a sauce helps it emulsify and coat the pasta smoothly.

content.text: Penne all'arrabbiata is a sauce with three ingredients: tomatoes, garlic, and chilli. The name means 'angry' and the sauce should taste sharp, hot, and clean. Do not add onion or cured meat: those belong to different sauces. The quality of the tinned tomatoes is what the dish rests on.

Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and chilli flakes. Cook gently for 2 to 3 minutes until the garlic is just beginning to turn golden at the edges. Do not let it brown: bitter garlic will ruin the sauce.

Add the tomatoes, crushing them with a spoon or your hands as they go in. Season with salt. Simmer uncovered for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened and the oil has separated to the surface. Taste: it should be sharp, hot, and concentrated.

Add the drained penne to the sauce with a splash of pasta water. Toss over high heat for 1 to 2 minutes until the pasta absorbs the sauce and everything is coated. Add parsley if using. Serve at once: arrabbiata waits for no one.

items.cause: The garlic browned or burned in the oil before the tomatoes went in
items.fix: Cook the garlic over medium, not high, heat. It should soften and turn pale golden: not brown. If it browns, discard the oil and garlic and start again.

items.cause: Not simmered long enough to evaporate moisture from the tomatoes
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for longer, 20 to 25 minutes if needed, until the sauce thickens and the oil separates to the surface.

items.cause: Pasta was drained and left sitting without sauce
items.fix: Move the pasta directly from the boiling water into the hot sauce, with a splash of pasta water, and toss immediately. Never rinse pasta.

items.cause: Chilli flakes were old or the quantity was too low
items.fix: Use fresh chilli flakes and taste the sauce before adding pasta. Add more chilli and simmer for another minute if heat is lacking.

content.text: Arrabbiata is a Roman sauce from Lazio. It is distinguished from other tomato-and-meat pasta sauces by the deliberate absence of onion and pork: the flavour comes only from the oil, garlic, chilli, and tomatoes. In Rome it is traditionally served with rigatoni rather than penne, but penne has become the standard outside Italy. The dish is eaten all over Italy as a fast weeknight supper with pantry ingredients.
